source.title: Automatically Interpreting Millions of Features in Large Language Models
source.authors: Gonçalo Paulo; Alex Troy Mallen; C. Juang; Nora Belrose

page_placements.theme: Dictionary features and other non-neuron directions (SAE, NMF, PCA, codes, CAVs, optimised neuron combinations) are more interpretable or concept-selective than native neurons

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether generated interpretations capture feature activity across contexts and reports that explanations based on top-activating examples can be less sensitive to the broader activation distribution. It also compares interpretation scores for SAE features and selected neurons, but does not test the Qwen3-32B pole audit or the stated neuron-explanation simulation claim.
record.gate_note: Relevant results include scores for interpretations generated using different activation-example sampling strategies, and scores comparing SAE feature interpretations with top-k neuron interpretations. Results about scoring-method correlations, costs, and intervention interpretation are not neuron-pole audit results. The study does not report proportions of neurons with one job, neuron simulation scores on new text, or attribution graphs.
record.test_reason: Only the neuron comparison bears on a version. Table A10 generates explanations for Gemma 2 9b and Llama 3.1 8b neurons from activating examples, then scores them with fuzzing and detection on 100 held-out activating and 100 non-activating examples. This is a different method from the original audit, aimed at whether explanations predict where neurons fire (V6). The study's main sampling experiments use SAE features, not neurons, so they fit no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors add that neurons score significantly lower than SAE features even when sparsified to the top-k active neurons. They also report that intervention scoring explains output features that context-based scores miss. Their main contribution is cheaper scoring methods (fuzzing, detection, embedding, surprisal, intervention) and sampling guidelines.
record.recipe_differences: The study generates and evaluates natural-language interpretations of SAE features, with a limited comparison to top-k neuron interpretations. It does not reproduce a neuron-pole audit; its key test uses interpretation scores across activating and non-activating examples and varies the sampling used to generate explanations.
record.method_sensitivity: Interpretation scores vary with activating-example sampling: top examples have lower fuzzing and detection scores than random or quantile sampling, while embedding scores show a different pattern. The paper also reports that sensitivity depends on activation degree and drops faster for top-example interpretations.

fits_no_version.finding: For Gemma 2 9b SAE features, explanations built only from top-activating examples score lower on fuzzing and detection than those from random or quantile samples (0.73 vs 0.76–0.77). Their accuracy drops more on low-activation deciles. Embedding scores show the opposite pattern.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Explanations of SAE features built from top-activating examples generalize less well across the activation distribution than those built from broader samples.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE features score well above top-k neurons on fuzzing and detection (e.g. 0.76 vs 0.62 in Gemma; 0.81 vs 0.55 in Llama).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In Gemma 2 9b and Llama 3.1 8b, SAE feature explanations predict activations far better than neuron explanations.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: The neuron comparison uses top-k neurons and reports aggregate fuzzing and detection medians, not neuron simulation scores or the fraction of neurons meeting a quality threshold. The central sampling comparisons are on SAE features, and the reported score medians are not direct estimates of the share of features or neurons that are interpretable. The paper also notes that context length and dataset sampling can leave some features inactive or underrepresented.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were left out. Other tables and figures report scoring-method correlations, scoring costs, or intervention interpretation scores rather than outcomes for the claim versions.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or job shares.
No shares of single-job neurons across models or MoE or trillion-parameter scale.
No share of interpretable neurons, no vision models, no architecture or regularization test. The top-32 vs top-256 sparsification change is small and not a tools test.
Not tested on Qwen3-32B neuron poles or by human inspection. Neuron layers and the exact neuron type are not stated.
Neuron explanations were scored with fuzzing and detection, not simulation. No fraction of neurons above a good-score threshold, and no explainer-strength comparison for neurons.

missing.what: SAE-feature scores alongside the neurons (e.g. 131k Gemma 0.76/0.74; 262k Llama 0.81/0.83), needed to put the neuron rows in context

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked the SAE sampling rows to V6 and the neuron rows to none. I reversed this, because V6 concerns neurons. The neuron rows directly show explanations from activating examples failing to predict held-out firing. 'Top k neurons' means only the k most active neurons per token are kept, a sparsified neuron basis. V7 is not credited because fuzzing is not simulation and no good-score threshold fraction is given, though the near-chance medians point the same way.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not audit Qwen3-32B neuron poles or report shares with one job, two jobs, or unknown jobs.

The study evaluates SAE features and selected top-k neurons in Gemma 2 9b and Llama 3.1 8b; it does not test whether the claimed neuron-pole shares hold across models, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, or models up to trillions of parameters.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron or recursive-generalization explanation is evaluated.

The study compares interpretation scores for SAE features and selected top-k neurons, but does not estimate the share of interpretable neurons or test the essay's InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates or its architecture/regularization explanation.
The study does not build or evaluate attribution graphs as circuit explanations.
The study tests SAE feature interpretations, not the specific Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit. Its sampling experiments do not establish how often this failure occurs across neurons or models.

Although the study reports fuzzing and detection scores for selected top-k neuron interpretations, it does not report simulation scores for neuron explanations on new text or the fraction of neurons passing a stated good-score threshold.

relation.reason: The comparison of neuron explanations in Table A10 gives results of its own that bear on V6.

tranche.reason: This is a different method on the same question: fuzzing and detection scoring of LLM explanations from activating examples, with a side comparison to top-k neurons. The study makes no argument that a version is wrong, so T5 does not fit.

source_check.notes: Table A10 explains top-k sparsified neurons, and the layers are not stated. The text does not say which example sampling the neuron explainer used. The record's 'code: n' is wrong: the paper releases the delphi library and reproduction scripts.

statements.correction: 2410.13928 code: y. The 'Data and Code Availability' section says the delphi library and reproduction scripts are released, and the abstract says the code is available online. Explanations are released via Neuronpedia.
statements.problem: The Table A10 numbers are right: Gemma 0.62/0.59 fuzzing and 0.59/0.57 detection, Llama 0.55/0.54 and 0.53/0.53, random 0.51, Llama 3.1 70b explainer and scorer (F.8). But the 'why' says 'code n' for 2410.13928, and the text says code is released.
Llama 3.1 70b is the explainer and scorer (F.8). Neuron explanations are only automated and never inspected by humans. Human explanations and ratings cover SAE features only.
Llama 3.1 8b neuron detection is 0.53 for both top-32 and top-256, against a random-interpretation baseline of 0.51 (Table A10).

statements.correction: Fig 2, Table A6 and F.3 vary the explainer's example sampling for the 131k Gemma 2 9b residual SAE features, with a Llama 3.1 70b explainer and scorer. Scoring is fixed at 100 activating examples (10 per decile) plus 100 non-activating ones. Fuzzing medians: top 0.73, random 0.76, quantiles 0.77. Detection: 0.72, 0.74 and 0.74. The authors add that scoring only on top-activating examples would hide this effect.
statements.problem: The finding is right, but it is filed under the factor 'Scoring set'. In 2410.13928 the sampling that varies is of the examples shown to the explainer. The scoring set is fixed, and the subjects are SAE features, not neurons.
Medians of 0.53–0.62 against 0.51 random match Table A10 for top-32 and top-256 neurons of Gemma 2 9b and Llama 3.1 8b.
All fuzzing medians in Table A10. Gemma: 131k SAE 0.76 vs top-32 neurons 0.62. Llama: 262k residual SAE 0.81 vs top-32 neurons 0.55. The MLP SAE scores 0.79. Detection shows the same gap.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Top-activating-example generation; fuzzing and detection evaluations
reader_labels.reason: Top-example interpretations score lower than interpretations generated from random or quantile samples on fuzzing and detection, and the paper explicitly says top-example interpretations have lower sensitivity and can miss the wider activation distribution (r7, r8, r10, r11).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Embedding evaluation and the second Appendix C example
reader_labels.reason: The top-example condition does not consistently underperform: it has a higher aggregate embedding score, and in the second example its fuzzing and detection scores exceed whole-distribution sampling (r9, r12, r13).
